(2) Track mtime for all three files — rejected as overengineered; reviews and errors are small files read on demand.

properties.title: Stub command registrations in CLI index for framework completeness
properties.context: The bead spec asks for stub registrations of sync, viz, and config commands so the CLI framework is complete, even though those commands are not yet implemented.
properties.decision: Registered all four commands (init, sync, viz, config) in the commander program. Stubs print a "not yet implemented" message with a reference to the relevant bead. All accept --json flag per project convention.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained a complete CLI help output and --json consistency; the stubs create dead code paths that could mislead users if they try to use them.
properties.alternatives: Could have omitted stubs entirely — rejected because the spec explicitly requests them and having the commander structure in place makes future beads easier.

properties.title: Use deprecated server.tool() API instead of registerTool()
properties.context: The MCP SDK v1.x provides both server.tool() (deprecated) and server.registerTool() for registering tools. Both work but have different call signatures.
properties.decision: Used server.tool(name, description, zodSchema, callback) — the deprecated but stable API. The registerTool API requires a config object with inputSchema/outputSchema fields which has a different typing approach.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained simpler, more concise registration code that is well-documented in examples. Accepted use of a deprecated API that may be removed in SDK v2.
properties.alternatives: (1) registerTool() — the recommended replacement, but its typing with InputArgs generics was more verbose for no functional benefit in this use case. Would switch when the deprecated API is actually removed.

properties.title: MCP tool handlers return discriminated content blocks instead of direct values
properties.context: MCP tools need a standard response format that includes both data and error states. Could return values directly, throw exceptions, or use a wrapper structure.
properties.decision: All tool handlers return a unified response object with content[] array (containing type and text fields) and optional isError boolean. Error cases return JSON-serialized error objects with error code and message.
properties.tradeoffs: Requires JSON serialization of all results (even non-error cases). But this matches MCP protocol expectations and allows graceful error handling without exceptions.
properties.alternatives: Throwing typed errors from tools (rejected: interrupts MCP handler flow). Returning value | error union directly (rejected: no isError flag for callers). Custom error types (rejected: MCP expects JSON).

properties.title: whygraph_context uses exact ref matching without partial file path matching
properties.context: When getContext receives a file path, it must decide whether to match refs using exact equality or partial path matching (e.g., "component.ts" matches "src/ui/component.ts").
properties.decision: Refs match only on exact file equality. If file param is "src/ui/component.ts", only refs with that exact string match. Partial matching is not supported.
properties.tradeoffs: Cannot find nodes from shorthand paths. But exact matching is explicit and won't accidentally return unrelated nodes from other files. Callers can always try with full paths if needed.
properties.alternatives: Substring matching on basename (rejected: "button.ts" would match multiple files). Glob pattern matching (rejected: adds complexity). File path normalization + flexible matching (rejected: platform-dependent).

properties.title: whygraph_context includes file-level refs when symbol is requested
properties.context: When a caller requests getContext(file, "someSymbol"), a ref might exist for the file alone with no symbol. Should a file-level ref match when a specific symbol is requested?
properties.decision: File-level refs (refs with no symbol) are always included in matches even when a symbol is specified. A symbol-specific ref matches only if symbol matches exactly. This way, both file-level and symbol-level decisions are returned.
properties.tradeoffs: May return broader context than the caller expected (decisions on the whole file, not just the symbol). But missing file-level constraints is dangerous — a decision at file level applies to all symbols.
properties.alternatives: Only match symbol-specific refs when symbol is provided (rejected: loses file-level constraints). Return in separate buckets (rejected: complicates the API). Require explicit flag to include file-level (rejected: foot-gun by default).

properties.title: whygraph_context collects decisions from parent chain, not children
properties.context: When a component matches the file/symbol, getContext must decide which decisions are relevant: only on the component, on parents up to feature/app, on children, or some combination.
properties.decision: Relevant decisions are those with AFFECTS edges pointing to matched nodes OR any node in their parent chains (up to app). Child decisions are not collected.
properties.tradeoffs: Doesn't show decisions made on child components. But child-level decisions are less critical when working on a parent — parent-level decisions are binding constraints. Callers needing child context should query those nodes directly.
properties.alternatives: Include all descendants (rejected: too broad, makes output unwieldy). Only matched nodes (rejected: misses inherited constraints). Bidirectional traversal (rejected: overcomplicates the model).

properties.title: getDecisions uses OR logic for tag filtering
properties.context: When a caller provides multiple tags, need to decide if decision must match ALL tags or ANY tag to be included.
properties.decision: Tags use OR logic. If caller requests ["arch", "data"], a decision is included if it has either (or both) of these tags. Multiple tags in the filter means union, not intersection.
properties.tradeoffs: Less precise filtering when multiple tags are provided (more results). But AND logic is rarely useful for discovery — agents usually want "decisions about architecture OR data modeling", not decisions about both simultaneously.
properties.alternatives: AND logic (rejected: too restrictive for discovery). Separate AND/OR parameters (rejected: adds complexity). Individual tag requirements with operator (rejected: over-engineers the API).

properties.title: getDecisions filters status, date with AND logic but tags with OR logic
properties.context: When multiple filter types are provided (status + tags + date range), need rules for how they combine. Tags already use OR internally, but how do tags combine with other filters?
properties.decision: Different filter types use AND logic. If status="active" is provided with tags=["arch", "data"], results must match status AND have at least one tag. If date range is also provided, results must fall within the range AND match the other filters.
properties.tradeoffs: Requires understanding both AND (between types) and OR (within tags). But this aligns with how most query APIs work: filters narrow each other down, while options within a filter broaden it.
properties.alternatives: All AND (rejected: makes tag filtering too restrictive). All OR (rejected: no way to require a status). Separate "include" and "exclude" filters (rejected: over-engineered).

properties.title: Date filtering uses ISO 8601 string comparison, not parsed dates
properties.context: The date property is stored as ISO 8601 string. Could parse to Date objects for comparison or rely on string ordering.
properties.decision: Use direct string comparison with < and > operators. ISO 8601 dates sort lexicographically (YYYY-MM-DD), so "2026-03-20" < "2026-03-23" works naturally without parsing.
properties.tradeoffs: Breaks if dates are stored in non-ISO formats. But the type system enforces ISO strings (DecisionProperties.date is typed as string, not Date), so this is safe.
properties.alternatives: Parse to Date objects (rejected: overhead for a comparison that works with strings). Date library (rejected: unnecessary dependency). Epoch milliseconds (rejected: requires migration of existing data).

properties.title: getDecisions returns node IDs, not full decision objects
properties.context: Callers need decision identifiers to fetch full details or use in downstream operations. Could return full DecisionProperties or just IDs.
properties.decision: Returns array of decision node IDs as strings. Callers use these IDs to fetch full attributes via getNodeAttributes or to reference in staging entries.
properties.tradeoffs: Requires follow-up queries for full details. But IDs are lightweight and let callers fetch only the decisions they care about, avoiding payload overhead.
properties.alternatives: Return full decision properties inline (rejected: bloats response for discovery queries). Return id + title summary (rejected: forces a fixed summary format). Return promises for lazy loading (rejected: incompatible with JSON-based MCP).

properties.title: getGaps finds nodes with no inbound AFFECTS edges, not nodes with no associated decisions
properties.context: A node might lack recorded decisions because no one has documented them yet. Gap detection could search for nodes without any properties, or nodes without incoming AFFECTS edges from Decision nodes.
properties.decision: A gap is any Feature or Component node with zero inbound AFFECTS edges. This means no Decision nodes have an AFFECTS edge pointing to it. Not having properties or description is irrelevant — the gap is about missing documented decisions.
properties.tradeoffs: A node with full description and refs but no decisions is still a gap. The definition is strict (no AFFECTS edges). But this aligns with whygraph's core purpose: surfacing nodes that lack architectural decision capture.
properties.alternatives: Nodes with empty description or no refs (rejected: conflates documentation with decision capture). Nodes that appear in fewer than N decisions (rejected: arbitrary threshold). Nodes with no outgoing edges (rejected: wrong direction, would flag sinks).

properties.title: getGaps orders Features first, then Components by depth
properties.context: Gap detection returns a list, which could be unordered, alphabetical, by creation order, or by structural importance. Need a prioritization scheme.
properties.decision: Order is deterministic: (1) all Features first, (2) top-level Components (depth <= 1, direct children of features), (3) deeper Components. Within each tier, order is graph iteration order (stable but not controllable).
properties.tradeoffs: Does not sort alphabetically or by name within tiers. Graph iteration order is implementation-dependent and not user-visible. But hierarchical order is more important than alphabetic — features are more critical gaps than nested components.
properties.alternatives: Alphabetical (rejected: misses structural importance). Chronological (rejected: order of creation doesn't correlate with importance). Flat unordered (rejected: no guidance on where to start interviewing).

properties.title: getGaps defines component depth as distance to Feature or App in parent chain
properties.context: "Top-level" component is ambiguous. Could mean direct child of App, direct child of any Feature, or something else.
properties.decision: Depth is calculated by counting COMPOSES parent edges until a Feature or App is reached. Depth 1 = direct child of a Feature. Depth 2+ = nested under other Components before a Feature. App nodes are not counted in depth.
properties.tradeoffs: A Component with both Feature and Component parents (unusual case) stops at the first Feature encountered. Depth is absolute, not relative to query location. But this provides a clear structural ordering.
properties.alternatives: Depth only from App (rejected: would conflate Feature children with App children). Depth from any ancestor (rejected: ambiguous when multiple paths exist). User-configurable depth threshold (rejected: adds parameters).

properties.title: getGaps respects optional limit as a slice, not a page limit
properties.context: When caller provides a limit parameter, should it truncate the results or should it request paginated results beyond the limit?
properties.decision: The limit parameter is a hard truncation: gap results are ordered, sliced to limit, and returned. Calls with limit=10 return first 10 gaps (or fewer if fewer exist). No pagination info is returned.
properties.tradeoffs: No way to retrieve gaps beyond the limit in the same call. But pagination adds complexity and gaps are typically used for discovery (10-20 at a time is enough). Agents can re-call with no limit if needed.
properties.alternatives: Return pagination cursor (rejected: over-engineers for an interview tool). Return total count (rejected: requires full scan even when limit is applied). Ignore limit if it's > 100 (rejected: arbitrary boundary).

properties.title: whygraph_get_reviews returns all pending reviews from reviews.jsonl via MCP
properties.context: Reviews are stored in reviews.jsonl but agents running on non-local platforms (Cursor, Copilot) don't have filesystem access. Could expose via CLI only or make it an MCP tool.
properties.decision: Expose reviews via MCP tool whygraph_get_reviews with no parameters. The tool reads reviews.jsonl, deserializes all ReviewEntry objects, and returns the full array. Platform-agnostic access.
properties.tradeoffs: Agents must make an MCP call instead of reading a file directly. But this works uniformly across all platforms and keeps filesystem access centralized in the server.
properties.alternatives: CLI-only access (rejected: doesn't work for Cursor/Copilot agents). Filtered endpoint with query params (rejected: unnecessary complexity, reviews file is small). Streaming results (rejected: MCP doesn't support streaming for tool results).

properties.title: whygraph_get_errors returns all staging errors from errors.jsonl via MCP
properties.context: Staging validation errors are stored in errors.jsonl. Agents need visibility into failed entries to fix them. Could expose via CLI or MCP tool.
properties.decision: Expose errors via MCP tool whygraph_get_errors with no parameters. The tool reads errors.jsonl, deserializes all ErrorEntry objects, and returns the full array.
properties.tradeoffs: Agents must make an MCP call instead of reading a file directly. But this mirrors whygraph_get_reviews and keeps filesystem access in the server.
properties.alternatives: CLI-only access (rejected: doesn't work for remote agents). Errors endpoint with filtering (rejected: agents need all errors to understand the full failure picture).

properties.title: whygraph_get_reviews and whygraph_get_errors return empty arrays when files don't exist or are empty
properties.context: When reviews.jsonl or errors.jsonl don't exist (e.g., on first run), need to decide between returning an error or an empty result.
properties.decision: Both tools gracefully handle missing or empty files by returning an empty array []. No error is raised. This is idiomatic for "fetch all" endpoints — zero results means no reviews/errors, not a failure.
properties.tradeoffs: Callers cannot distinguish between "no reviews ever existed" and "file reading failed silently". But reviews and errors are always-recoverable — missing these files is a normal state on fresh setups.
properties.alternatives: Return error for missing files (rejected: breaks on first run). Return error object instead of array (rejected: inconsistent with full array response). Return object with count + items (rejected: adds structure for zero new info).

properties.title: ReviewEntry and ErrorEntry are returned with full properties, not summarized
properties.context: Reviews and errors contain nested structures (ReviewEntry has newDecisionId, existingDecisionId, sharedNodeIds; ErrorEntry has entry, error, file). Could return summaries or full details.
properties.decision: Return complete ReviewEntry and ErrorEntry objects as stored in the jsonl files. ReviewEntry includes id, newDecisionId, existingDecisionId, sharedNodeIds, and status. ErrorEntry includes entry, error, and file.
properties.tradeoffs: Response payload is larger. But agents need full details to create resolve-review staging entries (e.g., they need reviewId to write the staging action). Summaries would force follow-up queries.
properties.alternatives: Return summaries with IDs (rejected: requires additional queries to get decision IDs). Return different schema (rejected: makes it inconsistent with file storage). Nested expansion with query params (rejected: adds endpoint complexity).

properties.title: Allow affects in node_patched validation
properties.context: The cascade removal logic needs to emit node_patched events that update a decision's affects array when some (but not all) affected nodes are removed. The validator previously forbade patching affects, treating it as edge-managed.
properties.decision: Removed affects from PATCH_FORBIDDEN and added it to KNOWN_PATCHABLE in validate.ts. The cascade processor is the only producer of affects patches, so the semantic integrity is maintained by the processor itself.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained the ability to partially update decision affects during cascade removal. Lost the validator-level guard that prevented arbitrary affects modification — now any node_patched event can modify affects, not just cascade-generated ones.
properties.alternatives: Could have skipped validation for cascade-generated events entirely, but that would weaken the overall validation guarantee. Could have added a flag to bypass specific forbidden fields per-event, but that adds complexity for a single use case.

properties.title: Cascade function returns all removed node IDs alongside events
properties.context: The autoDismissForNodes function needs to know ALL removed node IDs (root, descendants, and orphaned decisions) to properly dismiss reviews. Previously, only the directly-requested root node IDs were passed, missing cascade-removed nodes.
properties.decision: Changed collectCascadeRemovals to return a CascadeResult struct with both events and allRemovedNodeIds. The caller uses allRemovedNodeIds for review auto-dismissal, ensuring reviews referencing any cascade-removed node (including orphaned decisions) are dismissed.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained complete review cleanup coverage. The return type is slightly more complex (struct vs plain array), but the struct is private to the module and self-documenting.
properties.alternatives: Could have extracted removed node IDs from the cascade events by filtering for node_removed event types, but that couples the dismissal logic to event structure and would miss edge cases if event generation changes.

properties.title: BFS with depth tracking for leaf-first node removal ordering
properties.context: The spec requires node_removed events in children-first, parent-last order. The original DFS-based Set iteration produced nodes in traversal order (parent first), which is the opposite of what's needed. Additionally, the root node_removed was emitted by entriesToEvents before cascade events.
properties.decision: Switched to BFS with a depth map, then sort nodes by descending depth for removal. The root node_removed is now included in cascade output (not in entriesToEvents), and doProcess strips root node_removed from validEvents when cascade handles it. Events are assembled in strict order: node_patched, edge_removed, node_removed.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained correct event ordering that matches the spec and ensures graph projection can apply events without dangling references. The BFS + sort approach is O(n log n) vs the previous O(n) iteration, but n is bounded by graph size which is small.
properties.alternatives: Could have used DFS post-order traversal to get leaf-first ordering directly, but BFS with explicit depth is easier to reason about and debug. Could have kept root node_removed in entriesToEvents and reordered at the end, but splitting the responsibility makes the ordering harder to verify.

properties.title: Dependency injection for sync command testability
properties.context: The sync command needs interactive prompts (via `prompts` library) and console output, both of which are difficult to test in unit tests without mocking globals or capturing stdout.
properties.decision: Introduced a `deps` parameter on `runSync` with injectable `prompt`, `log`, and `logJson` functions. Production code uses defaults (console.log, prompts), tests inject mocks.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained full testability without vi.spyOn on globals or capturing stdout. Lost some simplicity in the function signature — callers must understand the deps parameter exists even though it has defaults.
properties.alternatives: Could have used vi.mock to mock the prompts module and console.log at the module level — rejected because module-level mocks are brittle and couple tests to import paths. Could have used a class with methods to override — rejected because the project uses named exports and functions, not classes.

properties.title: Reuse findWhygraphDir from sync command instead of duplicating directory traversal
properties.context: Config command needs to locate the .whygraph directory by walking up from the current directory. The sync command already has this logic exported as findWhygraphDir.
properties.decision: Imported and reused findWhygraphDir from sync.js rather than writing a standalone version in config.ts.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained single source of truth for directory discovery. Lost the ability to change config's lookup behavior independently — but there is no scenario where the two should diverge.
properties.alternatives: Duplicating the traversal logic in config.ts was rejected because it creates a maintenance burden and divergence risk for identical behavior. Extracting to a shared utils module was considered but premature — only two consumers exist.

properties.title: Separate runSync from registerSyncCommand
properties.context: The sync command needs both a commander integration point and a testable core function. The spec says "do NOT modify src/cli/index.ts" — the wiring will happen later.
properties.decision: Exported `registerSyncCommand` for commander wiring and `runSync` as the testable core. `runSync` takes a start directory and options, returns a typed `SyncOutput`. `registerSyncCommand` is a thin wrapper that calls `runSync` with `process.cwd()`.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained clean separation — tests exercise `runSync` directly without commander. Lost nothing significant, though there's a thin untested layer in `registerSyncCommand` (commander action handler).
properties.alternatives: Could have exported only `registerSyncCommand` and tested through commander's parseAsync — rejected because it would require mocking process.argv and make tests slower and more fragile. Could have exported just a raw function without the commander wrapper — rejected because the caller explicitly asked for a function they can wire into commander.

properties.title: SyncOutput type mirrors ProcessResult with success and message
properties.context: The --json flag needs structured output. ProcessResult from processor.ts has counts but no success/failure indicator or human message. The CLI layer needs to add those.
properties.decision: Created SyncOutput interface that spreads ProcessResult fields plus `success: boolean` and `message: string`. The `buildOutput` function converts ProcessResult to SyncOutput. Both JSON and human output use the same SyncOutput — JSON serializes the whole object, human output prints just the message.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained a single output type that serves both --json and human modes. Lost the ability to have richer human output that differs from JSON structure — but this matches the project convention that --json gives the same information as human output.
properties.alternatives: Could have returned ProcessResult directly and added success/message only for JSON — rejected because it would create two divergent output paths. Could have used a generic Result<T> wrapper — rejected as overengineering for a single command.

properties.title: Validate all flags before writing any changes (atomic validation)
properties.context: When a user passes multiple flags (e.g. --autonomy manual --sync-trigger bogus), partial writes are dangerous — the config would be left in a half-updated state that the user did not intend.
properties.decision: Collect all validation errors upfront before touching the config file. If any flag is invalid, no changes are written and all errors are reported at once.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained atomicity — config is never left in a partially-updated state. Lost the ability to apply valid flags while reporting invalid ones, which some CLIs do. The atomic approach is simpler to reason about and avoids surprising partial state.
properties.alternatives: Apply-what-you-can-and-warn was rejected because partial config updates are confusing — the user expects either all changes or none. Per-flag sequential validation with early return was rejected because it only reports the first error, hiding others.

properties.title: Use existing type system values (ask/never) instead of task-spec aliases (on-demand/off)
properties.context: The task spec mentions --context-injection values "always, on-demand, off" and --environment value "generic", but the established type system in core/types.ts uses "always, ask, never" and "other". These types are used across init, sync, and the broader system.
properties.decision: Used the existing type values (ask, never, other) as the canonical flag values. The config command validates against the same union types that the rest of the system uses.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained type safety and consistency with the rest of the codebase — no mapping layer needed, no risk of a value slipping through that downstream code cannot handle. Lost alignment with the task spec's exact wording, but the spec's values were aspirational aliases, not established contracts.
properties.alternatives: Adding a mapping layer (on-demand -> ask, off -> never, generic -> other) was rejected because it creates a divergence between what the CLI accepts and what config.json stores, which is confusing when users hand-edit the file or read it programmatically. Changing the core types was rejected because it would require updating init, sync, and all tests.

properties.title: Track and report changes as from/to pairs rather than just listing updated keys
properties.context: The config command needs to confirm what changed. Simply listing "updated: autonomy" is insufficient — the user needs to see what the old value was to verify correctness, especially in --json mode where scripts may consume the output.
properties.decision: Each change is recorded as a ConfigChange with from and to fields. The human-readable output formats as "key: old -> new" and the JSON output includes the full changes object.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained auditability — both humans and scripts can verify exactly what changed. Added slight complexity to the output type. The no-op case (setting a value to what it already is) is cleanly handled by omitting unchanged keys from the changes map.
properties.alternatives: Returning only the final config without change tracking was rejected because it forces the caller to diff against the previous state. Returning a flat list of changed keys without values was rejected because it is insufficient for programmatic consumers.

properties.title: Resolver uses discriminated union return with error accumulation
properties.context: The resolver must process a batch of staging entries where some may fail to resolve while others succeed. Need to decide between throwing on first error vs accumulating errors.
properties.decision: resolveEntries returns a ResolveResult with separate resolved[] and errors[] arrays. Failed entries are skipped (not added to resolved) and their error is recorded. This lets the caller process valid entries while reporting all problems.
properties.tradeoffs: Callers must check both arrays — slightly more complex API. But the alternative (throwing) would abort the entire batch on one bad reference, losing all valid work.
properties.alternatives: Throw on first error (rejected: loses valid entries). Return entries with null IDs for failures (rejected: pushes error handling to every consumer). Result type with ok/err per entry (rejected: over-engineered for the current need).

properties.title: Snapshot-per-unique-timestamp granularity for timeline scrubbing
properties.context: The bake engine needs to produce snapshots for the timeline slider. Events can share timestamps (e.g., a node_added and edge_added in the same operation). The question is whether to create one snapshot per event or one per unique timestamp.
properties.decision: Group events by unique timestamp and produce one snapshot per unique timestamp. Each snapshot replays all events up to and including that cutoff via buildGraphAt, yielding the full graph state at that moment.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained: timeline slider has meaningful steps that correspond to logical operations, not individual low-level events. The snapshot count stays manageable. Lost: if two events at the same timestamp produce meaningfully different intermediate states, that intermediate is invisible to the user.
properties.alternatives: One snapshot per event — rejected because it inflates snapshot count without adding useful visual information, and same-timestamp events are logically atomic. Fixed-interval sampling — rejected because it would miss events in sparse timelines and over-sample dense ones.

properties.title: Four-tier reference resolution order: alias, app, UUID, file-path
properties.context: A reference string in a staging entry could be an alias, the literal "app", a UUID, or a file path. Need a deterministic resolution order.
properties.decision: resolveRef checks in order: (1) alias map, (2) "app" literal, (3) UUID regex match, (4) file-path ref lookup in graph. First match wins.
properties.tradeoffs: An alias named "app" would shadow the built-in app resolution — but "app" is a reserved word in practice. A UUID-formatted alias would be treated as UUID first, but aliases should be human-readable names, not UUIDs.
properties.alternatives: Require prefixes like @alias or $app (rejected: adds syntax overhead to the staging format). Check graph existence for UUIDs before accepting (rejected: new nodes created in the same batch won't be in the graph yet).

properties.title: Inline D3 from node_modules rather than bundling or CDN
properties.context: The baked HTML must be self-contained (openable offline, no network dependency). D3 v7 is already a dependency in package.json. Options: inline from node_modules, embed a vendored copy, or reference a CDN with fallback.
properties.decision: Read d3.min.js from node_modules/d3/dist/d3.min.js at bake time and inject the full script content into the template. The path is resolved relative to the compiled module location using __dirname.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained: zero network dependency, guaranteed version match with package.json, single self-contained HTML artifact. Lost: HTML file is ~300KB larger due to inlined D3; bake requires node_modules to be installed.
properties.alternatives: CDN with local fallback — rejected because offline-first is a hard requirement for baked artifacts. Vendored copy in src/viz/ — rejected because it duplicates what npm already manages and creates version drift risk.

properties.title: File-scoped alias map reset per resolveEntries call
properties.context: Aliases allow entries within a staging file to reference each other by short name. Need to decide alias scope boundaries.
properties.decision: The alias map is created fresh in each resolveEntries call and not persisted. Aliases defined in one call are invisible to other calls. This enforces file-scoped isolation since each staging file is parsed and resolved independently.
properties.tradeoffs: Cannot reference aliases across staging files. But cross-file aliases would create implicit ordering dependencies between files, making the system fragile.
properties.alternatives: Global alias registry persisted across calls (rejected: creates ordering dependencies). Alias resolution as a separate pre-pass (rejected: unnecessary complexity when single-pass works).

properties.title: Template uses literal placeholder tokens replaced by string substitution
properties.context: The HTML template needs slots for dynamic content (snapshots JSON, baked-at timestamp, review count, D3 script). Options: use a template engine (handlebars, ejs), use tagged template literals in code, or use simple string markers replaced via String.replace.
properties.decision: Used double-percent delimited tokens (%%SNAPSHOTS%%, %%BAKED_AT%%, %%REVIEW_COUNT%%, %%D3_SCRIPT%%) in the HTML file, replaced by String.prototype.replace() in bakeViz. No template engine dependency.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained: zero additional dependencies, template is valid HTML readable by any editor, replacement logic is trivial and testable. Lost: no escaping or sanitization — if snapshot JSON contained the literal string %%BAKED_AT%% it would be double-replaced. No conditional or loop constructs in the template.
properties.alternatives: Handlebars/EJS — rejected because adding a template engine dependency for four substitutions is excessive. Template literals in TS — rejected because it makes the HTML unreadable and uneditable outside of code, and prevents designers from working on the template independently.

properties.title: Accept UUID-format references without graph existence check
properties.context: When resolveRef encounters a UUID-format string, it could validate that the node exists in the graph or accept it on format alone.
properties.decision: UUID-format strings are accepted without requiring the node to exist in the graph. This is necessary because a new node created earlier in the same batch (e.g., a feature) assigns a UUID that won't be in the graph until events are emitted.
properties.tradeoffs: A typo in a UUID will not be caught at resolve time — it will only fail at event emission or projection. But requiring graph existence would break the common pattern of creating a node and immediately referencing it.
properties.alternatives: Two-pass resolution where new nodes are added to a virtual graph first (rejected: duplicates projection logic). Require aliases for all intra-batch references (rejected: UUIDs from the existing graph should work directly).

properties.title: serializeGraph uses graphology forEachNode/forEachEdge iteration with type assertions
properties.context: graphology's forEachNode and forEachEdge callbacks receive loosely-typed attributes (Attributes = Record<string, unknown>). The code needs to produce VizNode[] and VizEdge[] with required label fields. The spread of attributes onto the object includes label from the graph (set during projection), but TypeScript cannot verify this statically.
properties.decision: Used `as VizNode` and `as VizEdge` type assertions on the spread objects. The projection module (buildGraphAt) guarantees that label is set on every node and edge because it comes from the event data, so the assertion is safe at runtime.
properties.tradeoffs: Gained: clean compilation without changing graphology's type definitions or adding runtime validation overhead. Lost: if projection ever stops setting label, the type assertion would mask a runtime bug. The assertion is a contract with projection.ts.
properties.alternatives: Runtime validation with throws — rejected because it would add error paths for a condition that cannot happen given correct event data, and the viz layer should not re-validate what core already guarantees. Wrapping graphology with stricter generics — rejected because CLAUDE.md says "graphology is the graph — do not build parallel data structures."

properties.name: MCP Server
properties.description: stdio-based MCP server exposing whygraph tools (context, decisions, gaps, reviews, errors) with staleness detection

properties.name: Projection
properties.description: Pure functions that replay WhyEvent arrays into graphology MultiDirectedGraph instances, supporting full replay and time-travel (cutoff) queries.

properties.title: Pure functions taking graph as first argument
properties.context: The query layer needs access to the projected graph. Could inject it via class, closure, or pass explicitly.
properties.decision: All query functions are pure — they take a MultiDirectedGraph as the first argument and return results with no side effects.
properties.tradeoffs: Slightly more verbose call sites, but enables trivial testing (pass any graph) and no hidden state.
properties.alternatives: A Query class wrapping the graph; module-level singleton; dependency injection container.

properties.title: Symbol matching semantics in getContext
properties.context: When getContext receives both file and symbol, we need rules for which refs match. A ref might have file only, or file+symbol.
properties.decision: A ref matches if (1) file matches AND ref has no symbol (file-level ref always matches), or (2) file matches AND symbol matches. This means a file-level ref is a broad match, while a symbol-specific ref is narrow.
properties.tradeoffs: A file-level ref matches even when a specific symbol is requested, which could return extra nodes. But omitting file-level matches would hide relevant context.
properties.alternatives: Strict match requiring exact symbol; ignore symbol parameter entirely; require all refs to have symbols.

properties.title: Collect decisions from matched nodes and their parent chains
properties.context: getContext must decide which decisions are relevant. Decisions could be collected from only the matched nodes, or from the full ancestor hierarchy.
properties.decision: Relevant decisions are those with AFFECTS edges pointing to any node in the set of matched nodes PLUS all nodes in their parent chains. This captures both local and inherited architectural context.
properties.tradeoffs: May surface decisions that feel tangential (e.g., a decision on a parent feature). But missing inherited constraints is worse — a junior might violate a feature-level decision while working on a child component.
properties.alternatives: Only collect from matched nodes; walk the entire subtree downward as well; let callers specify depth.

properties.title: getGaps excludes App and Decision nodes
properties.context: getGaps finds nodes without inbound AFFECTS edges. App nodes never have AFFECTS edges (they are structural roots). Decision nodes are the source of AFFECTS, not targets.
properties.decision: Only Feature and Component nodes are considered for gaps. App and Decision nodes are filtered out.
properties.tradeoffs: If someone adds a new node label, they must update getGaps. But including App/Decision would produce meaningless noise.
properties.alternatives: Include all node types; accept a label filter parameter.

properties.title: Hierarchical gap ordering by label then COMPOSES depth
properties.context: getGaps returns nodes ordered by importance. Features represent larger architectural gaps than deeply nested components.
properties.decision: Order is: Features first, then top-level Components (direct children of Features via COMPOSES), then deeper Components. Within each tier, order is graph iteration order.
properties.tradeoffs: Does not sort alphabetically or by creation date within tiers. Graph iteration order is stable but not user-controllable.
properties.alternatives: Sort by name; sort by number of descendants; flat alphabetical; let caller sort.

properties.title: Date comparison uses string ordering on ISO dates
properties.context: getDecisions filters by after/before on the date property. Dates are stored as ISO strings (YYYY-MM-DD).
properties.decision: Use direct string comparison (< and >) for date filtering. This works because ISO 8601 date strings sort lexicographically.
properties.tradeoffs: Breaks if dates are stored in non-ISO formats. But the type system enforces ISO strings via DecisionProperties.date.
properties.alternatives: Parse to Date objects; use a date library; store as epoch milliseconds.

properties.title: Synchronous lock-then-async pattern for processor pipeline
properties.context: The processor needs to hold an advisory lock during the entire pipeline execution. proper-lockfile returns an async release function, but internal operations mix sync (loadEvents, appendEvents) and async (clearErrors, writeErrors, file deletion) calls.
properties.decision: Acquire lock at top level in processStaging(), delegate all pipeline work to a separate doProcess() async function, release in finally block. This separates lock lifecycle from business logic cleanly.
properties.tradeoffs: Two-function split adds a level of indirection; could have used a single withLock pattern like sessions.ts does
properties.alternatives: withLock helper wrapping entire pipeline (sessions.ts pattern); manual try/finally inlined in single function

properties.title: Global type-priority sort across all staging files before resolution
properties.context: Multiple staging files may contain entries that reference each other via aliases. A component in file1.md might reference a feature alias defined in file2.md. Resolution requires all features to exist before components are resolved.
properties.decision: Collect all entries from all files into a single array, sort by type priority (feature=0, component=1, ..., node-removed=7), then resolve as one batch. This guarantees cross-file alias resolution works correctly.
properties.tradeoffs: Loses per-file ordering — entries within the same type priority are not guaranteed to preserve their original file order. This is acceptable because same-type entries should not depend on each other's aliases.
properties.alternatives: Process files independently (breaks cross-file aliases); topological sort based on alias dependencies (over-engineered for the constraint that aliases are file-scoped in resolver)

properties.title: Cascade removal collects all descendants then generates edge removals before node removals
properties.context: When a node is removed, its COMPOSES descendants and their edges must also be removed. Graphology's dropNode removes edges automatically, but event sourcing requires explicit edge_removed events.
properties.decision: Recursively collect all COMPOSES descendants into a set, generate edge_removed events for ALL edges touching any removed node, then generate node_removed events for descendants. The original node's removal is handled by the main event stream, not the cascade function.
properties.tradeoffs: Generates edge_removed events even for edges that graphology would auto-remove — this is necessary for event log completeness but adds event volume
properties.alternatives: Only remove nodes and let projection handle implicit edge removal (breaks event sourcing contract); remove edges one-by-one during traversal (risk of visiting already-removed edges)

properties.title: Dedup uses timestamp+type+id signature matching against all existing events
properties.context: If the processor crashes after appending events but before deleting staging files, re-running would produce duplicate events. Need a dedup mechanism for crash recovery.
properties.decision: Build signatures from timestamp|type|id for all existing events, skip new events whose signature matches. This is simple and catches exact duplicates from replayed staging files with fixed timestamps.
properties.tradeoffs: Only catches exact matches — if timestamps are auto-generated (no fixed timestamp in staging entry), new UUIDs from resolver mean dedup won't trigger. This is acceptable because auto-timestamped entries represent genuinely new work.
properties.alternatives: Content-hash dedup (expensive, over-broad); idempotency keys in staging entries (requires parser changes); append-then-compact (adds complexity)
